lines: h1
Point to the tooth that hurts.
h2
It's the first thing a dentist asks. And it sounds like the easiest question in medicine.
h3
But when the pain is coming from deep inside the tooth, patients point to the right one only about thirty percent of the time.
h4
So why is your brain so bad at finding a toothache?
e1
In 2010, endodontists at the University of Minnesota asked seventy-nine emergency patients to do exactly that.
e2
Overall, they picked the right tooth about seventy-three percent of the time.
e3
But split the patients into two groups, and a pattern appears.
e4
When the inflammation had spread to the tissues around the root, they were right eighty-nine percent of the time.
e5
When the pain was still confined to the inside of the tooth? Just thirty percent.
a1
To understand why, you have to look inside the tooth.
a2
At its center is the pulp: a soft core of blood vessels and nerves.
a3
Those nerves come in two main kinds. Fast A delta fibers, which fire a sharp, quick jolt. And slow C fibers, which produce that dull, throbbing ache.
a4
What the pulp doesn't have are proprioceptors, the sensors that tell your brain exactly where something is happening.
a5
The ligament around the root is different. It's packed with mechanoreceptors that track pressure on the tooth with remarkable precision.
a6
So once inflammation reaches that ligament, the tooth starts to hurt when you bite. And suddenly, the patient can point right at it.
a7
A 2007 study in San Antonio found this tenderness when biting in fifty-seven percent of patients with irreversible pulpitis.
w1
There's a second problem. And it's in the wiring.
w2
Pain signals from your teeth, your skin, your jaw muscles, and even your neck all flow into the same relay station in the brainstem.
w3
In 1986, Barry Sessle's lab at the University of Toronto recorded single neurons in that relay station, in cats.
w4
They found that single neurons there responded to several sources at once: a tooth, the skin of the face, the lining of the mouth, and the muscles of the jaw and neck.
w5
It's like a switchboard where many lines share a single operator. A signal arrives, but the brain has to guess which line it came from.
w6
When it guesses wrong, we call it referred pain.
s1
And the worse the pain gets, the less reliable that guess becomes.
s2
In 1984, Yair Sharav and colleagues at the Hebrew University mapped the pain of one hundred ninety-six dental patients.
s3
The more intense the pain, the farther it spread. And pain from upper and lower teeth overlapped so much that its location alone could not identify the source.
s4
In 1996, a team at the University of Kentucky asked four hundred patients with back-tooth pain to draw it on a diagram of the head.
s5
Again, stronger pain meant more referral. The researchers pointed to an overexcited nervous system, where pain neurons start responding to a wider and wider area.
l1
Even in a perfectly controlled lab, the problem doesn't go away.
l2
In 2025, researchers at the University of Dundee sent tiny electrical pulses into specific upper teeth of nineteen volunteers, and asked them to point.
l3
For front teeth, they were right about two-thirds of the time. For back teeth, it was closer to a coin flip.
c1
That's why endodontists don't just trust where a patient points.
c2
They reproduce the pain instead. Cold tests, tapping, bite tests, sometimes selective anesthesia, until one tooth gives itself away.
c3
The patient tells you that something hurts. The testing tells you where.
c4
So if you've ever struggled to tell which tooth is aching, it isn't you. It's how your nervous system is wired.
